purpose: Naratriptan is used to treat migraine headaches once they have already started. It helps relieve the pain, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound that come with migraines. It is not used to prevent migraines or to treat other types of headaches.
how_it_works: During a migraine, certain blood vessels in your brain widen and cause pain. Naratriptan works by tightening those blood vessels back to their normal size. It also blocks pain signals from being sent to your brain, which helps stop the migraine.
common_side_effects: You may feel tingling, warmth, or a flushing sensation in your face, neck, or chest. Some people feel drowsy, dizzy, or slightly nauseous after taking it. A mild feeling of tightness or pressure in the chest or throat can also occur.
warnings: Do not take naratriptan if you have heart disease, a history of stroke, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or certain types of migraines called hemiplegic or basilar migraines. Tell your doctor if you are taking antidepressants, as combining them can cause a rare but serious condition called serotonin syndrome. Seek emergency help right away if you have severe chest pain, shortness of breath, or sudden weakness after taking this medication.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 1 mg or 2.5 mg taken by mouth as a tablet when your migraine begins. If your migraine comes back after it improved, you may take a second dose at least 4 hours after the first. Do not take more than 5 mg in a 24-hour period. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
